title: How are two overlapping circles related to the idli-vada game?
description: Two circles hold the multiples of three and the multiples of five up to sixty. The overlap holds the numbers where idli-vada is said, and a count of both circles checks the picture.
teaching_notes: One idea: the overlap of the two circles is where idli-vada is said. Watch for the multiple of three, six, which belongs in the left circle only.

source: Figure it Out box 1, Q4, p.108
video_script.why: The child places the multiples of three and five up to sixty in two overlapping circles and sees that the overlap is where idli-vada is said.
video_script.substitution: Put the numbers in both lists in the overlap, and the rest in their own circle.
video_script.anchor: children playing the idli-vada game, drawn as two overlapping circles up to sixty
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, idli-vada is said in the overlap, which holds fifteen, thirty, forty five and sixty

final_answer.value: Yes; the overlap is where idli-vada is said: 15, 30, 45, 60
final_answer.spoken: yes, idli-vada is said in the overlap, which holds fifteen, thirty, forty five and sixty

hold_back: said in the overlap, which holds
never_show: any number outside 15, 30, 45, 60 in the overlap
maths_rules: left circle: multiples of 3; right circle: multiples of 5
the overlap holds the multiples of both: 15, 30, 45, 60
check: 16 + 4 = 20 multiples of 3 up to 60; 8 + 4 = 12 multiples of 5 up to 60
the printed figure (game till 30) leaves 6 out of the left circle; 6 belongs there
video_script.design: One idea: the overlap of two circles is the set of numbers in both lists, which is where idli-vada is said. Same method as the earlier example: write both lists, then place the common numbers in the overlap.
